How the opening has changed

The whole first paragraph on 2015-01-01, 2019-01-01, 2023-01-01 and in the version analysed here (2026-11-03), as each read. Press Play on a version to watch the one before it turn into it: words taken out fade in red, words added appear in green. Above each, the short description: the line Wikipedia shows under the title in its search box and apps. Until about 2018 that line came from Wikidata, not from the article, so older versions often show none here. Under every paragraph, short description changes: each change to that line made since the column before (Play steps the line through them, with their dates, while the paragraph changes) (checked through the page history from 2017, when articles began to set it themselves; how); changes put back within a day are folded. Sources cited opens, under every column, the footnotes placed inside that first paragraph, read the same way as the article's, with today's ratings; many first paragraphs cite nothing, because Wikipedia's guideline lets the opening rest on sources cited further down (the whole article's sources at each date are under Sources cited). Sentences that changed most opens three rows: today's three most-changed opening sentences, each traced back through every date (at each, the opening sentence with most words in common, by a fixed rule), and through the two template columns; Play on a sentence shows its change from the column before. How this is compared.

1 January 2015
126 words, 3 sentences
Short description: none

Buddhism is a nontheistic religion that encompasses a variety of traditions, beliefs and practices largely based on teachings attributed to Siddhartha Gautama, who is commonly known as the Buddha, meaning "the awakened one". According to Buddhist tradition, the Buddha lived and taught in the eastern part of the Indian subcontinent sometime between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE. He is recognized by Buddhists as an awakened or enlightened teacher who shared his insights to help sentient beings end their suffering through the elimination of ignorance and craving by way of understanding and the seeing of dependent origination and the Four Noble Truths, with the ultimate goal of attainment of the sublime state of Nirvana, by practicing the Noble Eightfold Path (also known as the Middle Way).

1 January 2019
97 words, 4 sentences
Short description: World religion, founded by the Buddha

Buddhism (, ) is the world's fourth-largest religion with over 520 million followers, or over 7% of the global population, known as Buddhists. Buddhism is an Indian religion and encompasses a variety of traditions, beliefs and spiritual practices largely based on original teachings attributed to the Buddha and resulting interpreted philosophies. Buddhism originated in ancient India as a Sramana tradition sometime between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, spreading through much of Asia. Two major extant branches of Buddhism are generally recognized by scholars: Theravada (Pali: "The School of the Elders") and Mahayana (Sanskrit: "The Great Vehicle").

70 words, 3 sentences
Short description: Indian religion or philosophy based on the Buddha's teachings

Buddhism ( , ), also known as Buddha Dharma and Dharmavinaya (), is an Indian religion or philosophical tradition based on teachings attributed to the Buddha. It originated in northern India as a -movement in the 5th century BCE, and gradually spread throughout much of Asia via the Silk Road. It is the world's fourth-largest religion, with over 520 million followers (Buddhists) who comprise seven percent of the global population.

Analysed version
107 words, 4 sentences
Short description: Indian religion and philosophy

Buddhism, also known as Buddhadharma and Dharmavinaya (), is an Indian religion and philosophy based on teachings attributed to the Buddha, a śramaṇa (wandering ascetic) and religious teacher who lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE. It is the world's fourth-largest religion, with an estimated 320 million to 540 million followers, representing approximately 4.1%–6.7% of the global population. It originated in the eastern Gangetic plain as a śramaṇa movement in the 5th century BCE, and gradually spread throughout much of Asia via the Silk Road. Buddhism has since played a significant role in Asian culture and spirituality, eventually spreading to the West in the 19th century.

Wikipedia's voice in the opening

Each sentence of the opening section checked against Wikipedia's neutrality policy. A sentence is marked (orange edge) when there is evidence it is contested (editors took it out for a day or more and put it back, tagged it as disputed, or argued over it on the talk page; or it uses a word from Wikipedia's own “Words to watch” guideline) and it is stated in Wikipedia's voice, naming no one who holds the view. That marks sentences to check against the rule, not a finding that a sentence breaks it. “With attribution” names the cited authors in front of the sentence by a fixed template; the last column shows the earlier wording of the same sentence as Wikipedia printed it on 1 January of 2015, 2019, 2023, with the works it cited then that are gone now. Nothing here is written by this project, and it proposes no edit to Wikipedia (how).

How the summary rows are calculated. For the sources in scope that have a score s (independent quality, 0 to 1; or audience leaning, −1 to +1), each cited c times: mean per source = (s1 + … + sn) ÷ n, each source counted once; mean per citation = (c1·s1 + … + cn·sn) ÷ (c1 + … + cn), each source counted as often as it is cited. Both cover only scored sources: the share of citations they cover is given beside them. The rows cover every citation in scope, not only the sources listed in the table.

Opinion and harder-to-check citations

Of the article's 679 citations: opinion, comment or blog section 1 (0%) · no web link 314 (46%) · book with no page number 4 (1%) · behind a paywall or registration 4 (1%). We spot opinion pieces from the web address (such as /opinion/ or a blog) or from the footnote's own label. A book counts as not in English when the footnote says so, or when Open Library lists the book only in other languages. No quote or translation means the footnote does not copy out the passage it relies on, so a reader who does not know the language cannot check it. Each of these makes a footnote harder to check, not wrong.

Links to check

Cited websites whose home page could not be read, or whose domain was registered after the article cited it. A site our program could not open may work fine in a normal browser: many sites turn away automatic visitors, and some block whole countries or networks. A website address registered after the article cited it may have a new owner, or the registration may simply have been renewed or moved; the site's title then and now is shown so you can compare. “Wikipedia's mark” is what the footnote itself says about its link: live, dead, usurped (Wikipedia's word for an address taken over by someone else), or nothing.

About the ratings: Wikipedia's own list (Perennial sources) rates about 530 sources that its editors argue about often. Most sources are not on it; that is not a bad mark.
  • The quality score (Lin and colleagues, 2023) runs from 0 to 1 and covers news websites. Books and journals have no score.
  • Audience leaning says who shares a website, not what it publishes: −1 means only Democrats shared it, +1 only Republicans, 0 both equally. Out of every 100 people sharing it, Republicans = (1 + score) ÷ 2 × 100, so −0.4 is about 70 Democrats to 30 Republicans. It comes from US Twitter users matched to voter records (DomainDemo, 2025; Robertson and colleagues, 2018) and covers only websites shared widely enough.
  • Few publishers have a recorded political affiliation, and those records are written by volunteers on Wikidata and Wikipedia.
  • The ratings are today's ratings, not the ratings when the footnote was added.
  • Links between organisations (owner, founder, member of) come from Wikidata, which anyone can edit. † marks a fact for which Wikidata gives no source.
